Long Day's Journey Into Night. Eugene O'Neill's masterwork, published posthumously in 1956, is a four-act family tragedy that unfolds over a single day in a Connecticut summer home. It traces the Tyrone family's unraveling as addiction, disease, regret, and hidden resentments surface, culminating in confession and despair.

The play is largely autobiographical. O'Neill drew directly on his own family's struggles with morphine addiction, tuberculosis, and failed dreams. The protagonist is not any single character but the family itself—the father James, the mother Mary who is addicted to morphine, and two sons, one tubercular and one an alcoholic drifter. The title echoes Dante's Inferno; the journey is downward, each act pulling the family deeper into honesty and pain.

When it premiered in 1956, after O'Neill's death, the play won the Pulitzer Prize and is now considered one of the greatest works of American drama. The dialogue is verbose and repetitive, mirroring the circularity of family trauma and the way grievances resurface without resolution. Most remarkable is how the action spans from morning to late night in almost real time, intensifying the sense of inexorable decline. Eugene O'Neill's work stands as the most personal and introspective of his career. It pioneered American realism on stage through its unsparing portrayal of family dysfunction. The Iceman Cometh, O'Neill's other masterpiece, similarly explores addiction and self-deception. Death of a Salesman and A Streetcar Named Desire are contemporary tragedies grounded in family failure and the rupture of American life.
